Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi
The award-winning journalist and artist talks about her first book. Plus, Carolina A. Miranda on two new Guadalupe Rosales tomes out this fall.

Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism , a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

In the News

M. John Harrison won the Booker prize for The End of Everything , and readers and literary critics are split. Some are thrilled to see a science fiction title nab the award, a first in its nearly six-decade history. But the shortlist included a few undeniable favorites, like Jamaican novelist Marlon James’s The Disappearers , and the prize committee has a tendency to favor White, male authors (shocker!). I plan to read both and make up my mind after; let me know your thoughts in the meantime.
Natalie Renganeschi is joining the Women’s Studio Workshop , a center for printmaking, bookbinding, and other paper-related arts, as executive director.
After five years, Michelle T. Boone is retiring from her post as president and CEO of the Poetry Foundation .
A Mario Vargas Llosa biography that was in the works for 13 years got dropped by Penguin for being what it deemed too critical of the Peruvian author.
A Truman Capote estate auction has a few odd items up for grabs, namely the ashes of his dog Maggie . The wonders of auction houses never cease.

blocks.text: Required Reading

Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, whose memoir was nominated for a National Book Award, has a must-read essay out about the US’s denial of the visitor visa he requested to attend the ceremony in New York City this Wednesday. [ New Yorker ]

If you’ve ever wanted to create a time capsule , Ashley Stimpson has some thoughts. She writes about the history of the practice, the slim odds that a time capsule will ever be found, and why you should make one anyway. [ Longreads ]

During her pregnancy, filmmaker Siraad Dirshe found solace in books like Sasha Bonét’s The Waterbearers , a reminder of the need to archive, narrate, and preserve stories of Black motherhood . [ Literary Hub ]

blocks.text: What We’re Reading

Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books As I rejoin the queue for the Valeria Luiselli book that expired on my Kindle — the Brooklyn Public Library doesn’t play about digital loans — I’ve added a romance novel to my rotation: Ali Hazelwood’s The Love Hypothesis (2021). It’s predictable, it’s corny, and it’s just STEM enough to make me feel like I’m learning something about scientific research funding and early-detection cancer biomarkers. Truly the perfect holiday-season read.

Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor I just got a copy of Min Jin Lee’s highly anticipated American Hagwon and 50 pages in, I’m already hooked. The third in her Diaspora Quartet , it follows a Korean family doing their best to assimilate and find their place at a hagwon , or cram school.
